title: Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew

concept.text: The innovation would be an evidence-based explanation of how the earliest massive black holes were born and accumulated their mass. It would distinguish the contribution of initial black-hole seeds from later growth through feeding on surrounding matter and merging with other black holes, and connect those histories to the development of their host galaxies. The central question is how black holes reached millions to billions of solar masses so early in cosmic history.

An observed mass does not uniquely reveal a black hole’s birth mechanism: different initial masses and subsequent growth histories can lead to similar endpoints. Other information, including host properties and surrounding gas, can help discriminate between explanations. Establishing the history of an early population therefore requires more than detecting an exceptionally massive object or measuring its mass accurately.

Methodological synthesis: the explanation should also account for observational selection—why some objects enter the measured sample while others remain unseen. Selection affects the population astronomers observe; it is distinct from the physical processes that produce an individual black hole’s mass. The supplied evidence does not document a quantitative treatment of these selection effects.

significance.text: Establishing the formation and early growth channels would resolve a major explanatory gap behind the first known luminous quasars and their host systems. The supplied ESA/Webb release describes the difficulty of growing very massive black holes quickly from small seeds. A convincing solution would explain which initial conditions and growth processes actually produced these objects, rather than merely showing that a particular history is theoretically possible.

The advance would also clarify the relationship between black holes and early galaxies, including whether some massive black holes preceded much of the development of their present hosts. Conditional synthesis: a sufficiently predictive explanation could turn early black-hole populations into tests of conditions in the young Universe. Its implications would depend on the channel established; evidence for direct collapse of gas and evidence for a primordial origin would carry different physical meanings.

Limits on the impact: multiple formation and growth channels may operate, and their relative importance may vary across the population. Explaining one class of objects would not automatically explain every early quasar, establish a universal sequence of black-hole and galaxy formation, or resolve all of galaxy evolution. These are limits on generalization, not reasons to discount a well-established channel.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is to distinguish competing birth and growth histories convincingly. A large seed followed by modest growth can resemble a smaller seed followed by more extensive growth, while feeding and mergers can further obscure the initial conditions. Even evidence favoring a heavy seed may leave different birth mechanisms open: the supplied QSO1 account discusses both primordial and direct-collapse possibilities.

Engineering and inference synthesis: progress requires joint measurements of black-hole masses, host properties and surrounding gas across an informative early population, with uncertainties carried into the comparison of competing histories. Concrete barriers include separating initial mass from accumulated growth, determining how much the conclusions depend on assumptions about feeding and mergers, and establishing whether available host and gas measurements discriminate among origins. More precise endpoint masses alone would not necessarily remove these ambiguities.

Population-analysis synthesis: another barrier is connecting the detected objects to the underlying population. A persuasive analysis must model detectability and sample selection, rather than treating unusually observable sources as automatically representative. The supplied material does not provide a selection function, a sufficient sample size, or a demonstrated method that resolves all these degeneracies.

current_state.text: In a release dated 27 May 2026, ESA/Webb reported a mass measurement of QSO1’s black hole of roughly 50 million solar masses, inferred from gas motions. The account combines the black-hole measurement with information about its host and gas composition to favor a large initial seed. The reported inference therefore draws on more than black-hole mass alone.

ESA/Webb presents alternative heavy-seed origins: a primordial black hole formed within the first second after the Big Bang, or a black hole formed somewhat later through direct collapse of a giant gas cloud. These are proposed histories compatible with the interpretation, not directly observed birth events or confirmed formation mechanisms. The result is significant evidence concerning one object; it does not uniquely identify its origin or establish the formation channel of the wider early population.

The release describes continuing analysis of similar objects to investigate whether massive black holes predate the galaxies in which they now reside. That ongoing investigation marks the distinction between a suggestive individual case and an established population result. The broader formation-and-growth explanation remains incomplete in the supplied evidence.

Evidence scope: the supplied review assessed a complete, internally identified ESA/Webb press-release extraction, with no reported extraction issues or truncation. The underlying linked research papers and figure contents were not supplied or inspected in that review. Consequently, the record supports attribution of the measurement and interpretation to ESA/Webb, but does not independently assess the papers’ methods or publication status. The empty freshness record also prevents a claim that this account captures all developments through November 2026; that limitation does not invalidate the dated May report.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: obtain independent measurements of a statistically informative early population, combining black-hole properties with host and gas information. Compare competing seed and growth histories under explicit assumptions about accretion, mergers and observational selection. The analysis should show which histories the observations distinguish, which remain compatible, and whether the data require multiple channels. These are proposed methodological criteria, not an established consensus standard; no sufficient sample size is specified by the supplied evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent population measurements constrain competing seed and growth histories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed predictive test: use the inferred channels to predict additional observations, then check those predictions against subsequently obtained data. Useful tests would concern measurable relationships among black-hole masses, host properties, gas characteristics and population abundance. Agreement should survive reasonable changes in uncertain growth and selection assumptions, or clearly identify the assumptions on which the conclusion depends.
completion_criteria.label: Inferred channels predict subsequent observations under explicit growth and selection assumptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should be able to reproduce the principal measurements and population conclusions using disclosed data, analysis methods and uncertainty treatment. The final claim should specify the epochs, mass ranges, host environments and detectable populations actually tested, and state what remains unconstrained. Finite observations can establish the demonstrated breadth of a channel and its contribution within that domain; they cannot establish literal universality across every early black hole.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible measurements and population conclusions with explicit observational limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis—AST-10, “Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory”: this concerns a new observational capability, whereas AST-13 concerns the historical explanation of early massive black holes. Their potential overlap would depend on whether AST-10 observes populations that constrain relevant merger and growth histories. Its title alone does not establish those target populations or technical capabilities. Opening the band would not automatically identify birth channels; that would require demonstrating how its measurements distinguish competing histories.

Roster-based synthesis—AST-06, “Map the cosmic dark ages and first luminous structures in three dimensions,” and AST-11, “Identify the first generation of metal-free stars”: both concern the environment in which early black holes emerged. Mapping early structures could provide contextual constraints, while identifying the first stars could bear on possible stellar-seed histories. These are potential relationships inferred from the titles. Neither achievement alone would establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew, and AST-13 would not substitute for either achievement.

Roster-based synthesis—AST-03, “Identify the physical constituent of astronomical dark matter,” and AST-05, “Detect and identify a primordial gravitational-wave background”: these could intersect with questions about the very early Universe if a primordial black-hole origin were established. The supplied QSO1 interpretation does not establish such an origin, identify the constituent of dark matter, or demonstrate a primordial gravitational-wave background. A shared interest in primordial physics does not make these concepts equivalent.

Roster-based synthesis—AST-07, “Discover a reproducible breakdown of general relativity near black holes”: this tests gravitational physics, while AST-13 reconstructs formation and growth. Difficulty explaining a black hole’s early mass does not by itself demonstrate a breakdown of general relativity. These remain distinct scientific objectives despite their shared focus on black holes.

The underlying research papers and figure contents were not assessed in the supplied review, leaving their detailed methods, uncertainty treatment and publication status unexamined here.

brief.title: How the first giant black holes formed and grew
possible: Looking into the young Universe, we could explain how black holes became so massive so quickly. Astronomers could separate how much mass they were born with from how much they gained by swallowing matter and merging with other black holes.
We could also work out how their growth fitted into the lives of their surrounding galaxies, including whether some black holes were already massive before much of their galaxy developed.
why: This would explain the origins of the enormous black holes already present early in cosmic history. It would connect their birth and growth to the development of galaxies and give astronomers a way to test conditions in the young Universe.

sources.who: Ignas Juodžbalis, Cosimo Marconcini and collaborators
sources.showed: The team used gas motions to measure QSO1’s black hole at roughly 50 million times the Sun’s mass. Its surrounding galaxy and gas composition favor a black hole that was massive from birth.
sources.quote: The IFU composition maps supported these results, showing that the gas throughout QSO1 is almost entirely hydrogen and helium, with very little of the heavier elements like oxygen that would be expected in a galaxy rich with stars and stellar debris.
sources.cited_for: QSO1 provides evidence that some early black holes began with a large mass.
sources.not_established: This individual object does not distinguish birth near the Big Bang from later collapse of a giant gas cloud.

sources.who: Madisyn Brooks, Jonathan R. Trump and collaborators
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team combined galaxies’ light measurements to find faint black hole activity. The inferred masses fit growth from small initial black holes left by stars.
sources.quote:
We
also derive BH mass upper limits for the stacks with no
detected broad Hαemission.
sources.cited_for: Fainter galaxies broaden the population studied beyond unusually conspicuous black holes.
sources.not_established: Compatibility with small initial black holes does not uniquely establish their birth or growth histories.

sources.who: Ignas Juodžbalis, Roberto Maiolino and collaborators
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team found black holes unusually massive relative to their galaxies’ stars, but consistent with nearby relationships involving stellar motions. Some identification methods would miss many of these objects because their gas contains few heavy elements.
sources.quote:
find that a significant fraction of our AGN would be missed by them due to low metallicity or lack
of high energy ionizing photons
sources.cited_for: Both the galaxy property used for comparison and the detection method affect population conclusions.
sources.not_established: These relationships do not reveal which birth mechanisms produced the black holes.

sources.who: Fan Zou, Elena Gallo and collaborators
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team found that an X-ray signal used to argue for a black hole born from collapsing gas in UHZ1 was not robustly reproducible. Additional observations did not strengthen the signal.
sources.quote:
Moreover, the hard X-ray signal does not grow with the
additional exposure, contrary to expectations for a steady source, indicating that any excess is not persistent.
sources.cited_for: A claimed example of birth through gas collapse depends on measurements that remain disputed.
sources.not_established: The reassessment does not rule out gas collapse as a birth mechanism elsewhere.

sources.showed: In a preprint, Kim and Im accounted for dust hiding a feeding black hole and revised its mass upward. Its feeding rate was consistent with the Eddington limit, a benchmark feeding rate.
sources.quote:
consistent with the accretion rate at the Eddington limit; in
other words, not in super-Eddington in a signiﬁcant manner.
sources.cited_for: Dust corrections can change conclusions about how rapidly black holes grow.
sources.not_established: This individual case does not determine how much unusually rapid feeding contributed to early black hole growth.

shown: Juodžbalis, Marconcini and collaborators have combined a direct mass measurement with clues from QSO1’s surroundings to argue that it began large. This goes beyond measuring a massive black hole alone, but its birth mechanism remains unresolved.

Population studies now reach fainter black holes and compare their masses with their galaxies. Brooks and collaborators’ preprint finds histories compatible with small beginnings, showing why the most conspicuous objects cannot stand for the whole population.
missing: A convincing separation of birth mass from later growth through feeding and mergers is still missing.
Population conclusions still need to account for which objects telescopes detect and which remain unseen.
No established explanation yet connects the competing histories to their relative contributions across early black holes.

milestones.label: Population measurements distinguish birth and growth histories
milestones.explanation: Independent measurements of black holes, their galaxies and gas would have to distinguish histories under explicit feeding, merger and detection assumptions. This would reveal which histories fit and whether several are needed.

milestones.label: Inferred histories predict new observations
milestones.explanation: Inferred histories would have to predict later observations, with agreement surviving reasonable changes in growth and detection assumptions or identifying its dependence on them. This would test their explanatory power.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results within stated limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce measurements and population conclusions using disclosed data, methods and uncertainties, with observational limits stated. This would establish how broadly the explanation holds.

uncertain: The population size and measurement precision needed to distinguish competing histories remain unclear.
Different birth and growth routes may dominate different groups of early black holes.

page.title: Origins and early growth of massive black holes
page.definition: An observationally established formation and growth history for massive black holes at redshift z>6, where cosmic expansion has stretched their light by more than a factor of seven. It distinguishes their initial seeds from mass gained through gas accretion and black-hole mergers.

goal.need: QSO1's dynamical measurements place a massive black hole in a system with little room for stellar mass. A preprint posted on 24 November 2025 detects broad hydrogen emission in five of 16 stacked galaxy bins, implying median black-hole masses of 10^5.21–10^6.13 solar masses compatible with stellar-remnant seeds. Explaining these observations requires separating initial mass from subsequent growth and accounting for the objects that observations select.

figures.caption: Dynamical constraints for Abell 2744−QSO1, one object.
figures.note: The mass estimate includes an inclination correction from three-dimensional gas-kinematic modelling.

completion.title: Population data distinguish the primary seeds and growth mechanisms of early massive black holes.
completion.criterion: Observations of a defined population at z>6 identify its primary seed-formation channel and determine the contributions of gas accretion and black-hole mergers to its mass growth. The inferred history accounts jointly for the measured mass distribution, accretion luminosities and merger observations after observational selection is included. This is an Atlas-defined qualitative test; the cited bodies provide no common numerical acceptance threshold.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, interpreting the combined formation-and-growth goals of Astro2020, LISA and Athena/WFI.
completion.basis: Astro2020 Appendix B, LISA's Science Requirements Document and Athena/WFI's science drivers were searched for an acceptance test, confidence threshold and required sample for establishing a combined seed-and-growth history; none was found. Their goals support identifying the primary seeding channel and determining growth mechanisms. Their observing targets constrain inputs to that inference.

milestones.title: A z>6 black hole has broad Hα with signal-to-noise ≥5 and ΔBIC>5.
milestones.criterion: Detect broad Hα, a hydrogen emission line, at z>6 using JADES's study-specific cuts: broad-component signal-to-noise ≥5 and ΔBIC=BIC(narrow)−BIC(narrow+broad)>5, excluding instrumental artifacts and testing outflow explanations. BIC is the Bayesian information criterion. The analysis finds 28 robust and two tentative Hα sources over z=1.7–7. Separately, the UHZ1 reassessment's version dated 31 August 2026, marked accepted for publication, finds its X-ray excess only 2.0–2.9σ across plausible reductions.
milestones.set_by: JADES collaboration, Section 3 of its published spectroscopic selection protocol; these are study-specific cuts.
milestones.threshold_quote: The lower floor for accepting the BLR model was $\Delta BIC>5$.

milestones.title: Gas kinematics favour an early black hole over a nuclear star cluster at >5σ.
milestones.criterion: An early galaxy's resolved gas motions favour a Keplerian point mass over the extended stellar alternatives tested in the published analysis. For QSO1, the one-dimensional comparison gives >5σ preference over a Milky-Way-like nuclear star cluster. The paper published on 27 May 2026 reports one object at z=7.04; its inclination-corrected three-dimensional model gives log10(M_BH/M⊙)=7.7±0.3. This establishes a dynamical mass without identifying the birth mechanism.
milestones.set_by: The dynamical point-mass test used in black-hole astronomy, applied by Juodžbalis and collaborators to QSO1; >5σ is their reported comparison against a specified stellar model.

milestones.title: Seed-black-hole binaries at z=10–15 have masses and distances measured with 20% fractional errors.
milestones.criterion: Observe a binary inspiral with source-frame mass between a few 10³ and a few 10⁵ solar masses at z=10–15, measuring source-frame masses and luminosity distance with 20% fractional errors. LISA's reference system has total mass 4,000 solar masses, mass ratio 0.2 and z=15, with signal-to-noise ≥10. These are observational requirements published on 14 May 2018; the cited sources report no qualifying observation.
milestones.set_by: European Space Agency LISA Science Study Team, Science Requirements Document, OR 2.1 and MR 2.1.

milestones.title: An X-ray census contains >400 active nuclei at z>6, including >20 at z>8.
milestones.criterion: An X-ray-selected census contains >400 active galactic nuclei at z>6, including >20 at z>8. These nuclei emit radiation powered by accretion onto central black holes. Athena/WFI specifies this sample to constrain seed formation and growth, sampling luminosities 10^43–10^44 erg s⁻¹ at z≈6–7. This is its 2016 survey-design target; the cited sources report no qualifying census.
milestones.set_by: Athena/WFI science team, Section 3.1 of Athena Wide Field Imager Key Science Drivers.
milestones.threshold_quote: > 400 AGN at z > 6 and > 20 AGN at z > 8

milestones.title: X-ray population measurements select a seed-and-accretion scenario at z≈6–8.
milestones.criterion: Compare an observed X-ray luminosity function—number density per luminosity interval—at z≈6–8 with predictions for seed formation and accretion, identifying the best-fitting scenario. Athena/WFI gives no statistical decision threshold. This constrains seed-and-accretion histories before the full mass-growth decomposition in the completion test. The Brooks preprint's optical stacked detections permit light seeds but do not perform this X-ray population test.
milestones.set_by: Athena/WFI science team, Section 3.1; its population-comparison target is qualitative.

not_found: No common acceptance threshold for an established population-level seed-and-growth history was found in Astro2020, LISA's requirements or Athena/WFI's science drivers.
Athena/WFI's scenario-comparison target specifies no likelihood-ratio or confidence threshold.
The full 2024 LISA Definition Study Report exceeded browser retrieval limits; the numerical LISA targets here come from the opened 2018 requirements.
The linked MNRAS paper on QSO1's gas composition could not be opened.

results.finding: Gas motions around one black hole in QSO1 imply a mass of roughly 50 million solar masses.
results.detail: The release reports Keplerian motion and contrasts it with a distributed stellar mass, but does not state the significance of a comparison with a nuclear star cluster.
results.quote: They found that not only is the black hole immense — roughly 50 million solar masses — it makes up an astonishing two-thirds of QSO1’s total mass.

results.finding: Broad Hα appears in 5 of 16 stacked spectra; the highest-redshift detection has median z=5.78.
results.detail: The detections are stacks, not individual z>6 black holes. The analysis requires 3σ rather than ≥5σ and ΔBIC>6; it tests outflows. The text also reports 4/16 detections in its fitting section.
results.quote:
In 5 of these stacks,
we find evidence for a broad Hαemission component,
with no corresponding broad [Oiii] component.

results.finding: The 5 stacked broad-Hα detections are consistent with light-seed growth at Eddington ratios of 0.1–0.5.
results.detail: The comparison uses optical stacked spectra and black-hole mass estimates, not an observed X-ray luminosity function. Heavy seeds with slower accretion also remain consistent with the detections.
results.quote:
We find that the median BH masses implied by our
BL AGN detections could be formed by light stellar rem-
nant seed (102 M⊙) growth models withf Edd = 0.1−0.5.

results.finding: JADES-GS-210600 has broad Hα at z=6.306, within a sample of 28 robust broad-line AGN.
results.detail: Its figure reports broad-component S/N=10 and ΔBIC=52. The selection excludes pixel-driven artifacts and tests for outflows.

results.finding: For one galaxy, UHZ1, the hard X-ray excess reaches only 2.0–2.9σ.
results.detail: The reassessment finds no robust X-ray detection. It does not report a broad Hα detection meeting the milestone’s signal-to-noise and ΔBIC cuts. An independent study also reported a nondetection.
results.quote:
Across all cases, we find only a marginal
signal in the hard band at the 2.0–2.9σlevel, substantially
less significant than the 4.2–4.4σreported by ´A. Bogd ´an
et al. (2024).

results.finding: Five secure z>6 broad-Hα sources include ID 5536, with broad-component SNR 27.41.
results.detail: ID 5536 is at z=6.222 and has ΔBIC=169.78 using the criterion’s sign convention. The study checks 1D and 2D spectra, accounts for the instrumental line-spread function, and tests outflow explanations using [O III] profiles.

results.finding: QSO1, one object: gas kinematics favour a point mass over a Milky-Way-like nuclear star cluster at >5σ.
results.detail: QSO1 is at z=7.04. The inclination-corrected 3D model gives log10(MBH/M⊙)=7.7±0.3. The dynamical measurement does not identify the black hole’s birth mechanism.
results.quote:
The evidence from kinematics alone corre-
sponds to >5σ preference for a point mass.
